title: Wessex
description: Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the south of Great Britain
wiki_lead:
The Kingdom of the West Saxons, also known as the Kingdom of Wessex, was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the south of Great Britain, from around 519 until around 927. In about  886, Alfred the Great adopted the title 'King of the Anglo-Saxons' as the ruler of all Anglo-Saxons not under Danish rule. Over the next thirty years Alfred's son, Edward the Elder and grandson Æthelstan conquered the Danish kingdoms, and when Æthelstan conquered the last surviving one, York, in 927, he adopted the title 'King of the English'. 
The Anglo-Saxons believed that Wessex was founded by Cerdic and Cynric of the Gewisse, though this is considered by some to be a legend. The two main sources for the history of Wessex are the West Saxon Genealogical Regnal List and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (the latter of which drew on and adapted an early version of the List), which sometimes conflict. Wessex became a Christian kingdom after Cenwalh (r. 642–645, 648–672) was baptised and was expanded under his rule. Cædwalla later conquered Sussex, Kent and the Isle of Wight. His successor, Ine (r. 689–726), issued one of the oldest surviving English law codes and established a second West Saxon bishopric. The throne subsequently passed to a series of kings with unknown genealogies.
During the 8th century, as the hegemony of Mercia grew, Wessex largely retained its independence. It was during this period that the system of shires was established. Under Egbert, Surrey, Sussex, Kent, Essex, and Mercia, along with parts of Dumnonia, were conquered. He also obtained the overlordship of the Northumbrian king. However, Mercian independence was restored in 830. During the reign of his successor, Æthelwulf, a Danish army arrived in the Thames estuary, but was decisively defeated. When Æthelwulf's son, Æthelbald, usurped the throne, the kingdom was divided to avoid war. Æthelwulf was succeeded in turn by his four sons, the youngest being Alfred the Great.
Wessex was invaded by the Danes in 871, and Alfred was compelled to pay them to leave. They returned in 876, but were forced to withdraw. In 878, they forced Alfred to flee to the Somerset Levels, but were eventually defeated at the Battle of Edington. During his reign Alfred issued a new law code, gathered scholars to his court and was able to devote funds to building ships, organising an army and establishing a system of burhs. Alfred's son, Edward, captured the eastern Midlands and East Anglia from the Danes and became ruler of Mercia in 918 upon the death of his sister, Æthelflæd. Edward's son, Æthelstan, conquered Northumbria in 927, and England became a unified kingdom for the first time. Cnut the Great, who conquered England in 1016, created the wealthy and powerful earldom of Wessex, but in 1066 Harold Godwinson reunited the earldom with the crown and Wessex ceased to exist.

grok_lead: Wessex, known as the Kingdom of the West Saxons, was a prominent Anglo-Saxon kingdom centered in southern England from its traditional founding around 519 until its integration into a unified England by the mid-10th century. Established by the chieftain Cerdic in the upper Thames Valley, it initially comprised territories in modern-day Hampshire, Wiltshire, and Dorset, expanding through conquests against British kingdoms and rival Anglo-Saxon states. Under kings like Ceawlin (r. c. 560â592) and Egbert (r. 802â839), Wessex grew into a major power, subduing neighboring regions and asserting dominance over much of southern Britain by the early 9th century. The kingdom's defining era came during the reign of Alfred the Great (r. 871â899), who defended Wessex against relentless Viking incursions, culminating in the decisive victory at Edington in 878 that forced the Danes to accept baptism and withdraw from Wessex proper. Alfred's reforms, including the establishment of burhs (fortified towns), a standing army, and naval defenses, not only preserved West Saxon independence but also positioned Wessex as the nucleus for English resistance and cultural revival, with advancements in law, education, and vernacular literature. His successors, including Edward the Elder and Ãthelstan, extended these gains by reconquering Danish-held territories in the east, achieving the first effective unification of England under a single monarch by 927. Wessex's royal house thus provided the dynastic continuity for the English monarchy until the Norman Conquest, despite later symbolic revivals in literature and regional identity.
